attacks.claim: The migration is not a rename. It adds a new empty column and drops `notes`, so every existing user note is destroyed on deploy. The PR says notes cannot be recovered elsewhere, so this is irreversible data loss.
attacks.evidence: ALTER TABLE user_recipes ADD COLUMN private_notes text; ALTER TABLE user_recipes DROP COLUMN notes;

attacks.claim: The down migration does not restore data. It recreates an empty `notes` column and drops `private_notes`, so any notes written after deploy are also lost. Because migrations run automatically on merge, there is no safe rollback path.
attacks.evidence: ALTER TABLE user_recipes ADD COLUMN notes text; ALTER TABLE user_recipes DROP COLUMN private_notes;

attacks.claim: The PR description says 'Pure rename, no data change', which the migration contradicts. The claim is load-bearing for the merge decision and must be corrected or the migration rewritten.
attacks.evidence: "Pure rename, no data change; the down migration restores the old name." versus the migration's ADD COLUMN / DROP COLUMN pair

attacks.claim: Cursor lookup uses `findIndex`, which returns -1 when the cursor row is missing (for example, the user unsaved that recipe between pages). `start` then becomes 0 and the client silently receives the first page again, which can loop or duplicate items.
attacks.evidence: const start = cursor ? rows.findIndex((r) => r.id === cursor) + 1 : 0;

attacks.claim: The query has no LIMIT, so every request loads the user's entire saved set (up to 200k+ rows, with a join and `private_notes` payloads) into memory before slicing a page. This cannot meet the 300ms p99 budget and is a memory risk on the API process.
attacks.evidence:

attacks.claim: Pagination is done in JS over the full result set, so page 1 costs the same as page N. Cost grows linearly with saved-recipe count, which is unbounded, and there is no keyset index use.
attacks.evidence: const page = rows.slice(start, start + limit);

attacks.claim: The cursor is only the row id, but the sort key is (saved_at, id). A keyset cursor should encode the sort tuple so the next page can be found with an indexed WHERE clause. As written, the cursor is not meaningful outside the in-memory list.
attacks.evidence: ORDER BY ur.saved_at DESC, ur.id DESC

attacks.claim: Deploy ordering is unsafe. Migrations run automatically on merge, so the old code still reading `notes` will error on any request between migration and code rollout, and there is no expand/contract sequence.
attacks.evidence: Migrations run automatically on deploy after merge to main.

attacks.claim: ABSENT: no evidence that other queries, jobs, or views reference `user_recipes.notes`. Any remaining reference will break at deploy. The diff touches only saved.ts.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: grep or search results for `notes` across the repo; diff contains only saved.ts and its test

attacks.claim: `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN` on a ~140M-row table takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. Within an explicit transaction, the lock waits on any open readers and blocks all traffic to the table while held.
Removing the `offset` parameter is a breaking API change. The PR gives no evidence that all callers have moved to `cursor`, and old clients sending `offset` will silently get the first page.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: confirmation that no other clients send `offset`; the diff removes req.query.offset handling entirely

attacks.claim: Test coverage misses the failure cases that matter: a cursor for a deleted or unknown row, an invalid cursor, and a saved_at tie across pages. The test fixture only covers the happy path.
attacks.evidence: expect(c.nextCursor).toBeNull();

attacks.claim: Renaming to `private_notes` is a naming convention only and enforces nothing. The saved endpoint now returns `private_notes` by default, and nothing in the PR blocks it from reaching shared views.
attacks.evidence: SELECT ur.id, ur.recipe_id, r.title, ur.saved_at, ur.private_notes
